newsitem.title: USA: Settlement talks, more lawsuits await tobacco shrs.
newsitem.headline: Settlement talks, more lawsuits await tobacco shrs.

text.p: Tobacco stocks will post short-term gains following Monday's pro-tobacco jury verdict in Florida, but they will remain volatile in the longer term as the industry continues to wrestle with its legal and regulatory problems, analysts said.

The industry is counting on Monday's verdict to strengthen its hand in litigation-settlement talks with state attorneys general. The verdict by a Jacksonville, Fla., jury, which found R.J. Reynolds not liable in the 1995 death of Jean Connor, sent stocks soaring late in the session on Monday.
"It puts (tobacco companies) in a good posture for settlement talks, and shows they can still win in court. That's very important," said Diana Temple, tobacco analyst at Salomon Brothers.
Meanwhile, tobacco companies must contend with federal agencies and public health advocates over lawsuits, regulation, advertising and nearly every other aspect of the business.
Temple said upcoming lawsuits, as well the progress of the settlement talks, could still be "a stumbling block" to the overall stability of tobacco stocks.
"I'm still concerned that we are going to have some negative surprises. Nothing ever goes as smoothly as you would like," Temple said.
Montana became the twenty-fifth state on Monday to sue the tobacco industry for state Medicaid funds spent on the medical treatment of smoking-related illnesses.
A group of attorneys general from those states are meeting this week in Dallas to continue talks geared at settling the onslaught of public and private trials, which together number in the hundreds.
Roy Burry, tobacco analyst at Oppenheimer & Co, said the decision will bolster the industry's side of the talks and noted it shows the national jury pool has not been muddied.
Smith Barney analyst Martin Feldman, who attended a significant portion of the trial, said the verdict returns some of the confidence tobacco firms have historically enjoyed in courtrooms.

Another Florida jury shook that confidence last summer when it awarded $750,000 in compensatory damages to a former smoker who sued Brown & Williamson, a unit of B.A.T Industries Plc and the nation's third-largest cigarette maker.
"Once again, the jury was prepared to bless the traditional defenses of the industry," Feldman said.

"There's a lot of goodwill trying to make these talks succeed. The talks are the bigger determinant of stock price values. I would argue that this verdict is good for the talks, but it won't have a particularly substantial effect."
George Pirrone, senior trader at Dreyfus Corp, was less optimistic.
"I don't see any great enthusiasm at this point," he said of the decision. "It's good news, but there's so much bad news out there, I don't know how much the stocks can go (up)."
